parts.doc:
One section: its label, trigger and panel go inside. It carries the section's
own `value`, which is the name the root's `value` matches against.

props.name: value
props.doc: This section's own name, and what the root's `value` names.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: This one section opens and closes for nobody.

parts.doc:
The panel. It stays in the page when its section is closed - `hidden` decides
whether it shows, never an arm - so focus, scroll position and the ids other
parts point at all survive a close.

The heading a section's trigger sits in. The APG asks for one, and it is what
names the panel: `accordion.itemcontent` points its `aria-labelledby` here.
A consumer's `onClick` runs after the section has opened or closed.

The accordion itself; every section goes inside it. It holds which section is
showing, and every other accordion part reads that from here rather than
keeping a copy.

props.name: value
props.doc:
Which section is showing. A plain string names one section; with `multiple`
it is the list of sections that are showing. Omit it and everything starts
closed.

props.name: multiple
props.doc: Several sections may show at once. Without it, opening one closes the rest.

props.name: collapsible
props.doc:
Whether the section that is showing may be closed again, leaving nothing
open. On by default, which is Qwik UI's own default.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing opens or closes while this is set.

props.name: disableUntilFound
props.doc:
Closed panels are hidden outright rather than with `until-found`, so the
browser's find-in-page cannot reach the text inside them.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when a person opens or closes a section. Omit it
and the accordion still works; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc:
A button. Give it `pressed` and it becomes a toggle button that reports
`aria-pressed` and flips on each activation; leave `pressed` off and it is an
ordinary button with no state of its own.

props.name: pressed
props.doc:
Provide it and the button becomes a toggle button: it reports `aria-pressed`
and flips on every activation. Omit it and this is a plain button, with no
pressed state for a reader to announce.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new state each time a person flips a toggle button. Omit it
and the button still flips; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc:
A plain `<label>`. It wires nothing on its own: `for` is passed straight
through, so the consumer decides what it names. A family that owns its own
control ships its own label part instead, already pointed at that control.

Content that is hidden from sight but still reached by screen readers and
still focusable. The clipping style is written inline and no class ships, so
no consumer stylesheet can collide with it.
Steps the month back one.

The month itself: the one surface, whether it is shown in place or revealed by
a `calendar.trigger`.

It is the group a reader announces, named by `calendar.title`, and it owns the
whole keyboard model - arrows walk days and weeks, `Home` and `End` reach the
week's ends, `PageUp` and `PageDown` step a month, and with Shift a year. Put
the title, the two month triggers, the weekday names and the days inside it.
Supporting text, named by the month's `aria-describedby` behind `calendar.error`.
The validation message, named by the month's `aria-describedby` ahead of `calendar.description`.

The element a form submits. It is clipped, out of the tab order and hidden from
readers, and it carries the chosen date as `yyyy-mm-dd` under the root's
`name`. A `multiple` or `range` calendar submits nothing through it.
Steps the month on one.

A real `<button>`, not a grid cell: the whole date is its name, so a voice
control user can say it and a reader conveys the day without depending on the
column it sits in. `aria-pressed` rather than `aria-selected`, which a button
does not support.

props.name: value
props.doc: Which day this is, as `yyyy-mm-dd`. One of `calendar.state().days`.

parts.doc:
A visible caption for the calendar. The month's group is named by
`calendar.title` rather than by this, so that the name a reader hears follows
the month on show.

A month of days a person can choose from.

It holds the date, the month on show and the day the keyboard is on, and it
draws nothing itself: put a `calendar.content` inside it, and inside that a
`calendar.title`, a `calendar.backtrigger`, a `calendar.forwardtrigger` and one
`calendar.item` per day of `calendar.state().days`. Add a `calendar.field` when
a form has to submit the date, and `popup` with a `calendar.trigger` when the
month should be revealed rather than always shown.

It reports `ui-disabled`, `ui-readonly`, `ui-required`, `ui-invalid`,
`ui-multiple`, `ui-range`, `ui-popup`, `ui-open` and `ui-closed` for styling.

props.name: value
props.doc:
The date chosen, as `yyyy-mm-dd`. An array of them under `multiple`, and
`{ start, end }` under `range`. Omit it and nothing is chosen to begin with.

props.name: month
props.doc:
The month on show, as any `yyyy-mm-dd` date inside it. Defaults to the month
today is in. Once somebody moves the month, this is no longer what is shown.

props.name: multiple
props.doc: More than one day can be chosen, and `value` is a list of them.

props.name: range
props.doc:
Two days bound a span, and `value` is `{ start, end }`. The first press sets
an endpoint and reports nothing; the second completes the span and reports
it once. Not to be set alongside `multiple`.

props.name: min
props.doc: The earliest day that can be chosen, as `yyyy-mm-dd`. Earlier days stay reachable and refuse to be chosen.

props.name: max
props.doc: The latest day that can be chosen, as `yyyy-mm-dd`. Later days stay reachable and refuse to be chosen.

props.name: unavailable
props.doc:
Days that cannot be chosen, as `yyyy-mm-dd`. They stay focusable so a person
reading with the keyboard can land on one and hear that it is unavailable.

props.name: startofweek
props.doc: Which weekday a row starts on, `0` for Sunday through `6` for Saturday. Defaults to `0`.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing can be chosen and no day is a tab stop.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: The days can be walked and read, and none of them will change the date.

props.name: required
props.doc: A date is needed before a form submits.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: The date chosen is not an acceptable one. Reported as `ui-invalid` and on `calendar.field`.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `calendar.field`.

props.name: popup
props.doc:
The month is revealed by a `calendar.trigger` rather than shown in place.
Escape and a press outside close it; choosing a single date closes it too,
while a range or a list of days stays open.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the whole date once a choice is complete - once per press for a
single date and for `multiple`, and once for a range, on the press that
completes it. Omit it and the days still work.

parts.doc:
The month and year on show, as text. With no children it draws that text
itself; give it children and they are shown instead.

It is announced when it changes, which is how moving the month is conveyed
without moving anybody's focus, and it is the name the month's group carries.
Reveals the month. Only for a root that was given `popup`.
Moves back one step. Labelled "Previous slide" unless you say otherwise.
Moves forward one step. Labelled "Next slide" unless you say otherwise.

One slide. It carries `role="group"` and `aria-roledescription="slide"`, or
`role="tabpanel"` when the carousel has a nav list to pick slides with.

props.name: value
props.doc: Names the slide. A `carousel.navtrigger` with the same value shows it. Required.

parts.doc: The row of slide pickers. `role="tablist"`.
One slide picker. `role="tab"` inside the nav list's `role="tablist"`.

props.name: value
props.doc: Names the slide this picker shows. Required.

parts.doc: Starts and stops autoplay. Its label says which one the press will do.

The carousel itself; the scroll area, slides, nav list and triggers go inside
it. It holds which slide is showing plus every setting the other parts read -
orientation, looping, autoplay, drag - so a trigger never carries its own copy.

props.name: value
props.doc:
The value of the slide showing now. A slide is named by its `value`, and
nothing counts positions for you, so name the slide that should show.

props.name: autoplay
props.doc: Slides advance on their own. Start it from a `carousel.playtrigger`.

props.name: draggable
props.doc: A drag moves the slides. Omit it and dragging is on.

props.name: align
props.doc: Where a slide comes to rest in the viewport. Omit it and slides rest at the start.

props.name: rewind
props.doc: Moving past the last slide lands on the first. Omit it and the ends stop.

props.name: loop
props.doc: The slides run in an endless ring. Omit it and the ends stop.

props.name: autoplayInterval
props.doc: How long each slide is shown while autoplay runs, in milliseconds.

props.name: sensitivity
props.doc: How far the slides travel for a given drag distance.

props.name: move
props.doc: How many slides a back or forward trigger moves.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: Which axis the slides run along. Omit it and they run left to right.

props.name: mousewheel
props.doc: The wheel moves the slides. Omit it and the wheel scrolls the page.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the new value whenever the showing slide changes.

parts.doc: The window the slides move behind, and the element a drag is measured on.
The carousel's heading. Mounting it names the carousel for a screen reader.

Supporting text beside the checkbox, named by `checkbox.trigger`'s
`aria-describedby`. Mount it alongside `checkbox.error` and the trigger names
both, the error first.

The validation message, named by `checkbox.trigger`'s `aria-describedby` ahead
of `checkbox.description`. Mounting it is what marks the checkbox invalid -
`checkbox.trigger` reports `aria-invalid` for as long as this part is in the
page - so render it only when there is an error to show.

The visually hidden native input that carries the checkbox into a form. It
takes no configuration of its own: `name`, `value` and `required` come from
`checkbox.root`, so one place decides what a form receives.

The check mark. Its children render only while the checkbox is on or mixed,
and the element is `aria-hidden`, so the state it draws is never announced a
second time.
The checkbox's label. Its `for` points at `checkbox.trigger`, so clicking the text toggles.

The checkbox itself; the trigger, label, description, error and field parts go
inside it. It holds the checked value and the form details that
`checkbox.field` submits, so one place decides what a form receives.

props.name: checked
props.doc: The value the checkbox shows. Omit it and the checkbox starts off.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can toggle the checkbox, and `checkbox.trigger` is disabled outright.

props.name: required
props.doc: Marks the hidden `checkbox.field` input required, so a form refuses to submit unchecked.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `checkbox.field`.

props.name: value
props.doc: Submitted instead of the browser default `"on"`.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Intended to be called with the new value when a person toggles the checkbox.
Omit it and the toggle still works; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: A consumer's `onClick` and `onKeydown` run after the checkbox has toggled.

The group's validation message. Mounting it marks the select-all's checkbox
invalid for as long as it is in the page; an item's own message goes in a
`checklist.error` written inside that item instead.

The visually hidden native input that carries the enclosing checkbox into a
form. It takes no configuration of its own: `name` and `value` come from the
part that roots the instance, so one place decides what a form receives.

Roots one item's checkbox instance. `value` is required, because it is what the
group's ticked set holds and what a form submits — position is never identity.

props.name: value
props.doc: This item's name in the group's ticked set, and what a form submits for it.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: This one item is locked. The root's own `disabled` locks every item regardless.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by a `checklist.field` written inside the item.

parts.doc: Supporting text for one item. It renders its children and changes nothing else.

One item's check mark. Its children render while that item is ticked, and the
element is `aria-hidden`.
One item's label. Its `for` points at that item's trigger, so clicking the text ticks it.

One item's checkbox. Ticking it updates the group's whole set, which is what
the select-all is computed from.
Names the group by naming the select-all trigger, whose id the family mints.

The group and the select-all's own checkbox root are one element: `role="group"`
plus the checkbox root's own behavior.

props.name: value
props.doc: The values that are ticked. Omit it and nothing is ticked.

props.name: values
props.doc: Every value the list offers. Select-all compares the ticked set against this.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can change any item, and the select-all is locked too.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Intended to be called with the whole new ticked set whenever an item or the
select-all changes. Omit it and the ticking still works.

parts.doc:
The one trigger that ticks or clears every item. It reports mixed while only
some items are ticked, but mixed is never somewhere a click lands: activating
it from mixed ticks everything.

The select-all's check mark. Its children render while the select-all is on or
mixed, and the element is `aria-hidden`.

The panel. It stays in the page when the collapsible is closed - `hidden`
decides whether it shows, never an arm - so focus, scroll position and the
ids other parts point at all survive a close. A closed panel carries
`hidden="until-found"` unless the root turns that off, which is what lets the
browser's find-in-page reach the text inside it and open the panel on a hit.

One trigger and one panel that shows or hides. It holds whether the panel is
open, and both other parts read that from here. An accordion is the many-panel
version of the same idea.

props.name: open
props.doc: Whether the panel is showing. Omit it and the panel starts closed.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing opens or closes while this is set.

props.name: disableUntilFound
props.doc:
A closed panel is hidden outright rather than with `until-found`, so the
browser's find-in-page cannot reach the text inside it.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when a person opens or closes the panel. Omit it
and the panel still opens and closes; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: A consumer's `onClick` runs after the panel has opened or closed.

The saturation-by-brightness plane. It is `role="group"` and renders its own two
one-axis `role="slider"` controls, because one element carries one
`aria-valuenow` — a single slider would leave brightness unreachable to anyone
adjusting it with a reader. Put a `colorpicker.thumb` with no `channel` inside
it as the visible marker.
The one surface both shapes use: in place when the picker is inline, revealed by the trigger under `popup`.
Supporting text, named by the area's `aria-describedby` after any error.
The validation message, named ahead of the description. `invalid` on the root is what marks the control invalid.
The element a form submits: an `<input type="text">`, clipped and out of the tab order.

A box a person types into. The graph writes attributes and an input's shown
text is its `value` property, so this part only exists because the write was
measured to re-display a box a person had already typed into - the gate is
`packages/vitest-browser/browser/colorpicker-gates`.

props.name: channel
props.doc: Which number this box carries. Omit it and the box holds the hex.

parts.doc:
A real `<button>` carrying `aria-pressed`, boxNamed by the colour and the value it
stands for. `aria-selected` is not supported on `button`, which is calendar's
shipped ruling applied unchanged.

props.name: value
props.doc: The colour this swatch chooses, in any notation `value` accepts.

parts.doc: Names the picker for a reader: `colorpicker.area` and `colorpicker.content` point their `aria-labelledby` here.

The colour picker itself; the label, the area, the rails, the swatches and the
form element all go inside it.

`value` is a seed, not a controlled mirror: once a gesture has run the picker
holds its own colour and the prop is never read again. Feeding every `onChange`
back into `value` is redundant rather than harmful — and it is what would make
the 8-bit hex quantisation visible, since `#5A8FB3` parses back a fraction of a
degree off the hue it was written from.

props.name: value
props.doc: The colour to start on: `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb()`, `hsl()` or `hsb()`, with or without alpha. Omit it and the picker starts white.

props.name: swatches
props.doc: The colours `colorpicker.state().swatches` hands back for the consumer to repeat over.

props.name: alpha
props.doc: Keep and show the alpha channel. HTML's own spelling, from `<input type="color" alpha>`.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can change the colour, and every control drops out of the tab order.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: The colour can be read but not changed.

props.name: required
props.doc: The form element must carry a colour before a form submits.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: Report the control as invalid. A prop, not a consequence of mounting `colorpicker.error`.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `colorpicker.field`.

props.name: popup
props.doc: The picker lives behind `colorpicker.trigger` instead of rendering in place.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the new colour every time it changes, including during a drag.

props.name: onChangeEnd
props.doc: Called once the change settles: the pointer released, the key that moved it, or a typed entry committed.

parts.doc:
Inside a rail this is that channel's control; inside the area it is the marker
the family positions and nothing more. One part rather than two because the
consumer writes the same tag either way - what it is follows from where it sits.

props.name: channel
props.doc: The rail this handle belongs to. Omit it inside `colorpicker.area`.

parts.doc:
One channel's rail and the hit area its pointer gesture runs on. The family
publishes `--colorpicker-start` and `--colorpicker-end` for the gradient rather
than painting one, so the stylesheet owns the look.

props.name: channel
props.doc: Which number this rail carries. Omit it and the rail is the hue rail.

parts.doc: Opens the popup shape. Only rendered when the root carries `popup`.
The colour as words and as hex, or whatever the consumer writes instead.

The list the options go in. Closed hides it, never detaches it - the input's
`aria-controls` points at this element - so an id, scroll position and the
highlight all survive a close.

Supporting text for the field, named by the input's `aria-describedby`. Mount
it alongside `combobox.error` and the input names both, the error first.

The validation message, named by the input's `aria-describedby` ahead of
`combobox.description`. It carries `role="alert"`, so a reader speaks it when
it appears. Unlike the other families, mounting it does not mark the field
invalid: `invalid` is a prop on `combobox.root`.

The visually hidden native `<select>` that carries the choice into a form. It
takes no configuration of its own: `name`, `required` and `disabled` come from
`combobox.root`, so one place decides what a form receives.

The text field, and the only tab stop in the family. It owns the arrow, Home,
End, Enter, Escape and Backspace keys; a consumer's own handlers run after the
family's. Filtering the option list from the typed text is the consumer's job.

One option. It never takes DOM focus - the caret stays in the input, and the
highlight is family state keyed by `value` - so a pointer or a script that
focuses an option puts focus straight back in the field.

props.name: value
props.doc: This option's value. Required: no index stands in for it.

props.name: label
disabled
props.doc: Nobody can choose this option, and the arrow walk steps past it.

parts.doc:
One option's chosen mark. It stays in the page and carries `ui-hidden` while
its option is not chosen, and it is `aria-hidden`, so the state it draws is
never announced twice.
The words shown for one option. Plain markup: it decides nothing on its own.
The combobox's name. Named by `aria-labelledby` from the input and the list.

A combobox is a text field with a list attached. It is NOT a select: DOM focus
never leaves the input, the highlighted option is family state rather than the
focused element, and printable keys belong to the field.

The root holds the family's configuration and renders `role="group"`, exactly
as Qwik UI's `HComboboxRootImpl` does.

props.name: value
props.doc:
The chosen option's value. A plain string in the ordinary case; with
`multiple` it is the list of chosen values. Omit it and nothing is chosen.

props.name: open
props.doc: The list is showing. Omit it and it starts closed.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can change the choice or type in the field.

props.name: required
props.doc: A choice is needed before the form submits.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: The control is in an invalid state, reported as `aria-invalid` on the input.

props.name: multiple
props.doc: More than one option can be chosen at a time, and `value` becomes a list.

props.name: removeOnBackspace
props.doc: Backspace in an empty field removes the last chosen value. `multiple` only.

props.name: loop
props.doc: The arrow walk wraps around the ends instead of stopping at them.

props.name: inline
props.doc:
The list is part of the page rather than a popup: it is always showing, and
nothing dismisses it. Spelled as a native-style boolean attribute,
never as a mode enum.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `combobox.field`.

props.name: placeholder
props.doc: The field's placeholder. The root's value wins over the input's own.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new selection when a person chooses or unchooses an option:
a string ordinarily, the whole list with `multiple`.

props.name: onInput
props.doc: Called with the field's new text every time a person types in it.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.doc: Called when the list opens or closes.

parts.doc: Deliberately not a tab stop: only the input is.
The day of the month, 1 to whatever the chosen month and year allow.

props.name: placeholder
props.doc: The text an empty box shows. Defaults to the box's own shape: `dd`, `mm`, `yyyy`.

props.name: showLeadingZero
props.doc: Show a single-digit day or month as `04` rather than `4`.

parts.doc:
Supporting text for the group, named by every box's `aria-describedby`. Mount
it alongside `datebox.error` and the boxes name both, the error first.

The validation message, named by every box's `aria-describedby` ahead of
`datebox.description`. Mounting it is what marks the boxes invalid - they
report `aria-invalid` for as long as this part is in the page - so render it
only when there is an error to show.

The element a form submits. It is clipped, out of the tab order and hidden
from readers, and it carries the whole date as `yyyy-mm-dd` under the root's
`name`.

The group's name: the element `role="group"` points its `aria-labelledby` at.
Three boxes have no single control for a `for` to point at, so the name is
carried by the IDREF rather than a `for`.
The month, 1 to 12.

props.name: placeholder
props.doc: The text an empty box shows. Defaults to the box's own shape: `dd`, `mm`, `yyyy`.

props.name: showLeadingZero
props.doc: Show a single-digit day or month as `04` rather than `4`.

parts.doc:
A date typed one part at a time, as three number boxes rather than one text
field. It is the group the three boxes sit in and the home of the date they
spell: put a `datebox.label`, a `datebox.dayinput`, a
`datebox.monthinput` and a `datebox.yearinput` inside it, in whichever
order the date should read, and a `datebox.field` when a form has to submit
it.

It reports `ui-disabled`, `ui-required` and `ui-empty` for styling, and it is
the element a reader announces as the group the boxes belong to.

props.name: value
props.doc: The date the boxes show, as `yyyy-mm-dd`. Omit it and they start empty.

props.name: min
props.doc: The earliest date the boxes will settle on, as `yyyy-mm-dd`.

props.name: max
props.doc: The latest date the boxes will settle on, as `yyyy-mm-dd`.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing can be typed in any box, and they all drop out of the tab order.

props.name: required
props.doc: A whole date is needed before a form submits.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `datebox.field`.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the whole date as `yyyy-mm-dd` whenever the boxes spell one, and
with `null` while they do not. Omit it and the boxes still work; the call
site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: The year.

props.name: placeholder
props.doc: The text an empty box shows. Defaults to the box's own shape: `dd`, `mm`, `yyyy`.

props.name: showLeadingZero
props.doc: Show a single-digit day or month as `04` rather than `4`.

parts.doc:
The region a file can be dropped onto. It carries no role and no tabindex on
purpose: dropping is a pointer enhancement and the browse button is the
keyboard route, so a second tab stop here would do nothing the button does not.
It reports `ui-dragging` and `ui-disabled`.

The real `<input type="file">`. It is clipped, `aria-hidden` and out of the tab
order, so nothing but the family and the picker ever touch it — but it is the
element that actually submits, and the family keeps its `files` in step with
the rows on the page, dropped files included.
One chosen file's row. Everything it shows comes from the `file` record it is given.

props.name: file
props.doc: The file this row shows.

parts.doc:
The button that takes the file it sits in off the list. It takes no id: the
item around it holds one. Give it an `aria-label` — the visible character is
usually a cross, which a reader would otherwise announce as "times".

The file's name. Leave it empty and it renders the name the record carries;
give it children and they are shown instead.
The upload's name. Its `for` points at the real field, which is what names it for a reader.

The upload itself; the label, the drop area, the browse button, the real field
and the list of chosen files all go inside it. It holds the restrictions and
reports `ui-disabled` for styling.

There is no `value` prop: a `FileList` cannot be built from markup, so the
chosen files always start empty and are only ever added by a person.

props.name: accept
props.doc: What the picker offers and what a drop is filtered against, e.g. `image/*,.pdf`.

props.name: multiple
props.doc: More than one file may be chosen; without it a new choice replaces the old one.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing can be chosen: the button is disabled and drops are ignored.

props.name: required
props.doc: A file must be chosen before a form submits.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by the real field the family renders.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the chosen files whenever they change.

parts.doc: The button that opens the file picker. This is the keyboard and reader route in.

The card. Unlike a tooltip's tip this is a surface a person can work in: put
links, buttons and images in it freely.

It carries no `role`. It is not a description of the trigger and not a dialog;
its contents are read as themselves. Nothing here writes `aria-describedby`,
which would flatten the whole card into one run-on string with every link
welded together and none of them reachable.

**Write it after `hovercard.trigger`.** A CSS anchor has to be laid out
strictly before the element that points at it. An ordinary in-flow trigger
satisfies that from anywhere in the markup, so the order is only advice -
until you absolutely position the trigger yourself, at which point a card
written first silently lands at its containing block instead of beside it. CSS
has no way to report that, so put the card last and the question never comes
up.

It stays in the page when the card is hidden - `hidden` decides whether it
shows, never an arm - because the trigger points at its minted id, because
`hidden` is what takes its links out of the tab order, and because an elevated
element removed from the document while showing leaves the overlay stack's
marks behind.

Its `position: absolute` and anchor binding live in the part's own scoped
stylesheet - your `style` and `class` compose untouched. Everything about
where the card lands - `position-area`, `@position-try`, `position-visibility`,
offsets - is your CSS, keyed off `ui-side`.

The hover card itself; the trigger and the card go inside it, in that order.
It holds whether the card is showing, how long the pointer has to rest or
focus has to stay before it shows, how long it lingers after the pointer
leaves, and which side it sits on.

The pointer and focus handlers live here rather than on the trigger, so moving
from the trigger into the card - with the pointer or with Tab - never counts
as leaving.

props.name: open
props.doc: Whether the card is showing. Omit it and it starts hidden.

props.name: delay
props.doc:
How long the pointer must rest on the trigger, or focus must stay on it,
before the card shows, in milliseconds. Omit it and it is 700. Focus waits
the same time as the pointer: a person tabbing through a paragraph of links
has declared no interest in any one of them.

props.name: closeDelay
props.doc:
How long the card stays after the pointer leaves, in milliseconds. Omit it
and it is 300. It is what lets the pointer cross the gap between the trigger
and the card without the card going away.

props.name: side
props.doc:
Where the card sits against the trigger. It is written on
`hovercard.content` as `ui-side`; the placement itself is your CSS.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when the card shows or hides, including when
Escape or a press elsewhere hides it.

parts.doc:
The link the card previews. It renders an `<a>` and only an `<a>`, because the
card is a shortcut to where the link goes: **never put anything in the card
that is not also behind the link.** That is what makes the family defensible
for a person on a touch screen, or reading with a virtual cursor, who will
never see the card at all - they follow the link and get everything.

It carries `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` pointing at the card, so a
reader is told the surface exists and can be entered. Tab from the trigger
moves into the card, because the card is the trigger's next DOM sibling and
nothing takes it out of the tab order.

It also carries the CSS anchor the card is placed against, declared in the
part's own scoped stylesheet - your `style` and `class` compose untouched.

The surface the items go in, `role="menu"`. It is never modal: it writes no
`aria-modal`, so the page behind it keeps its focus and is never made inert,
and a wheel does not dismiss it.

It stays in the page when the menu is closed - `hidden` decides whether it
shows, never an arm - because an enlisted element removed from the document
leaves the overlay stack's marks behind.

A region that opens the menu where the pointer is: right-click, a touch long
press, `Shift+F10` or the ContextMenu key on anything focused inside it.

It carries no role, no name and no ARIA state at all. `aria-haspopup` says a
control opens a menu when it is activated, which a region that answers a
right-click does not do, and a context menu is equally discoverable to
everyone without an announcement of its own (React Aria's reasoning, and
w3c/aria#1971 is the open discussion). Give `menu.content` an `aria-label`:
with no trigger there is nothing else to name the surface.

One command. Given `checked` it is a `menuitemcheckbox` that toggles without
closing; inside a `radio` menu it is a `menuitemradio`.

A disabled item is still reachable with the arrows and still announced - the
APG's rule, and the divergence from `select`, whose walk skips a disabled
option - it simply cannot be activated.

props.name: value
props.doc: Reported to `onChange` when this item is activated. Required: no index stands in for it.

props.name: checked
props.doc:
This item carries a checked state, so it renders as a `menuitemcheckbox`.
Which items ARE checked is `menu.root`'s `checked`; writing the prop is what
says this item has the state at all.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can activate this item; the arrows still land on it.

parts.doc:
An item that opens a submenu. It is the parent menu's item and the submenu's
trigger at once, so it is written inside the nested `menu.root` it opens,
beside that root's `menu.content`.

The menu itself. Everything the family renders goes inside it, and it is the
anchor scope the surface is placed within.

A submenu is a `menu.root` written inside another menu's `menu.content`: the
nested root starts a menu instance of its own, holding its own open state, its
own roving focus and its own `onChange`.

props.name: open
props.doc: Whether the surface is showing. Omit it and the menu starts closed.

props.name: checked
props.doc:
The values of the items that start checked - checkbox items, or the one
chosen radio item. The checked set lives here rather than on each item
because a radio choice unchecks its siblings, which is one decision about
the whole menu, and because a seed may only read its own component's props.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can open the menu, and no item may be activated.

props.name: loop
props.doc: The arrow walk wraps at both ends. Menus wrap; a listbox does not.

props.name: radio
props.doc:
The items of this menu are one radio group: each renders
`role="menuitemradio"`, and choosing one unchecks the rest. Without it an
item carrying `checked` is a `menuitemcheckbox` and the rest are plain
commands.

props.name: side
props.doc:
Where the surface is placed against the trigger. It is also written on
`menu.content` as `ui-side`, so styling can follow the placement.

props.name: delay
props.doc: How long a pointer rests on `menu.itemtrigger` before its submenu opens, in milliseconds.

props.name: closeDelay
props.doc: How long a submenu stays open after the pointer leaves it, in milliseconds.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the item's `value` when an item is activated - a command, a
checkbox item toggling, or a radio item being chosen. A submenu is its own
root, so its activations reach the callback written on the submenu's root.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.doc: Called when the surface opens or closes, including when Escape or a press outside closes it.

parts.doc:
The control the menu opens from, and the family's only tab stop. It declares
`aria-haspopup="menu"`, so a reader says a menu is there before it is opened.

The dimming layer, and the element that is actually elevated: it carries the
`overlay` mark, the `hidden` gating, and the dismissal reports the overlay
behaviour delivers. It wraps `modal.content` rather than sitting beside it,
so styling the layer and the dialog together is ordinary nesting.

A consumer's `onDismiss` runs after the family has applied its own policy, so
a handler can see which way the family went.
A consumer's `onClick` runs after the dialog has closed.

The dialog surface. It stays in the page when the modal is closed - `hidden`
on the backdrop decides whether it shows, never an arm - because the overlay
behaviour marks the background off an attached element and unmarks it the
same way. A surface that detaches while showing leaves the rest of the page
inert with nothing left to unmark it.
A sentence the reader announces after the name.

The dialog itself; the trigger, backdrop, surface and close control go inside
it. It holds whether the dialog is showing and whether this is an alert
dialog. The root renders no elevated layer of its own - `modal.backdrop` is
the element that is elevated.

props.name: open
props.doc: Whether the dialog is showing. Omit it and the dialog starts closed.

props.name: alert
props.doc:
An alert dialog: it announces as `alertdialog`, it refuses to close on an
outside press, and opening it puts focus on the close control rather than
on the surface. Escape still closes it.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when the dialog opens or closes - including when
a dismissal closes it. Omit it and the dialog still opens and closes; the
call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: The dialog's name. Mounting it is what names the surface.
A consumer's `onClick` runs after the dialog has opened.

One top-level entry. It wraps either a plain `navbar.itemlink` or a
`navbar.itemtrigger` and the `navbar.itemcontent` that trigger shows, and it
is the element the pointer enters and leaves, so moving from a trigger down
into its own dropdown never counts as leaving.

props.name: value
props.doc: Names the item. The root's `value` names the item whose dropdown shows. Required.

props.name: active
props.doc:
This entry leads to the section a person is in. It writes `ui-active` for a
stylesheet and nothing else: the ARIA for "the page you are on now" belongs
on the one link that is that page, which is `navbar.itemlink`'s `current`.

parts.doc:
One dropdown. It stays in the page when it is closed - `hidden` decides
whether it shows, never an arm - so the trigger's `aria-controls` never
dangles and the focus, scroll position and form state inside a panel survive a
close.

A consumer's `onKeydown` runs after the family's.

A navigation link. It works at the top level of the navbar and inside a
dropdown, and it is the only part that can carry `aria-current="page"`.

props.name: current
props.doc:
This link is the page a person is on now. It writes `aria-current="page"`,
which the aria-at disclosure-navigation plan makes a priority-1 assertion.
Set it on the one link that is the current page, never on the whole section.

parts.doc:
The button that shows and hides one item's dropdown. `aria-expanded` says
which way it is, `aria-controls` names the panel by a minted id.

A consumer's `onClick` and `onKeydown` both run after the family's.

The `<nav>` landmark that holds the site's primary navigation.

It is a landmark, so it needs a name, and this family writes none: a page can
carry a primary nav and a footer nav, and an invented "Navigation" on both is
two landmarks a reader cannot tell apart. `{...rest}` is spread first, so
`<navbar.root aria-label="Primary">` is the whole story.

The family is a DISCLOSURE, never a menubar. `role="menubar"` puts screen
readers into application mode and promises desktop-menu behaviour that site
navigation does not have; the authoring practices, the aria-at plan and every
surveyed library agree that navigation is a set of buttons that show and hide
panels.

props.name: value
props.doc:
Which item's dropdown is showing, named by that item's `value`. Omit it, or
pass the empty string, and every dropdown is closed.

One value on the root rather than an `open` flag per item, because opening
one dropdown closes the others and only a value the whole navbar shares can
say that.

props.name: hover
props.doc: Dropdowns open when the pointer rests on an item. Omit it and they do.

props.name: delay
props.doc:
How long the pointer must rest on an item before its dropdown opens, in
milliseconds. Omit it and it is 200. It applies to the first dropdown only:
once one is showing, moving to another opens it at once.

props.name: clickGrace
props.doc:
How long after a dropdown opened under the pointer a click on the same
trigger is ignored, in milliseconds. Omit it and it is 300. Without it the
click that lands while the pointer is resting shuts the panel it just
opened.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the value of the item now showing its dropdown, or the empty
string when everything closed. Omit it and the navbar still opens and
closes; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc:
The one real text input: everything a person types goes here, which is what
makes paste, one-time-code autofill, undo and a single tab stop free. It is
invisible and stretched over the whole root, so a click or tap anywhere on the
boxes lands on it. `value` and `style` are the family's, so a consumer cannot
set them here; `pattern` and everything else an `<input>` accepts reaches the
element through the spread.

One box of the code. It draws its own character and reports `ui-empty` and
`ui-disabled` for styling, and it is `aria-hidden`: the boxes are decoration
over the single real input, which is what a reader announces instead.

props.name: index
props.doc:
Which character of the code this box shows, counting from 0. Writing the
boxes is what sets the length of the code: six boxes, a six-character code.

parts.doc:
A caret slot inside a box, for the consumer to style. It carries no state of
its own: the surrounding `otp.item` is what reports `ui-empty` and
`ui-disabled`.

The box the field is stretched over, so `style` is the family's: it is what
makes the field measure itself against this element rather than the page.
Everything else about the look of the boxes belongs to a consumer's class.

props.name: value
props.doc: The code entered so far. Omit it and the field starts empty.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing can be typed while this is set.

props.name: shiftPWManagers
props.doc:
Keep a password manager's icon off the boxes. Omit it and the icon is
pushed past the right edge, which is what most code fields want.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the whole code every time it changes, not with the character typed.

props.name: onComplete
props.doc: Called once with the whole code the moment it holds one character per box.

parts.doc: Steps to the previous page. Natively `disabled` on page 1.
Steps to the next page. Natively `disabled` on the last page.

One page's box, and the part that declares WHICH page this row of the anatomy
stands for. The control inside it - an `itemtrigger` or an `itemlink` - reads
that page number back off the item and carries the ARIA for it, so the number is
written once, on the wrapper.

props.name: value
props.doc: Which page this box stands for, counting from 1.

parts.doc:
The same control as `itemtrigger` over an `<a>`, for pagination that is real
navigation with real URLs. An anchor has no `disabled` attribute, so an
unavailable link reports `aria-disabled` and stays in the tab order.

The control inside a `pagination.item`. It takes no page number of its own:
the enclosing item already declared one, and this part reads it back to decide
where a click goes and whether it is the current page.

A consumer's `onClick` runs after the page has already moved.

The `<nav>` landmark that holds the page controls. It is a landmark, so it
carries a name: `aria-label="Pagination"` by default, and a consumer's own
`aria-label` replaces it - a page with a site nav, a breadcrumb and a
pagination has three navigation landmarks, and a reader lists them by name.

props.name: count
props.doc:
How many pages there are in total - pages, not rows. How many rows fit on a
page is the consumer's data layer, and a component told about the data twice
can disagree with itself.

props.name: page
props.doc: Which page is showing, counting from 1. Omit it and it starts at page 1.

props.name: siblingCount
props.doc:
How many pages to show on each side of the current one when the family
computes its range. Omit it and it is 1.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nothing navigates while this is set, and every control reports unavailable.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new page number when a person moves to another page. Omit it
and the pagination still moves; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: A consumer's `onClick` runs after the popover has closed.

The surface. It is not modal: it carries no `aria-modal`, so the page behind it
stays reachable, keeps its focus, and is never made inert.

It stays in the page when the popover is closed - `hidden` decides whether it
shows, never an arm - because an elevated element removed from the document
while it is showing leaves the overlay stack's marks behind.

A consumer's `onDismiss` runs after the family has closed the popover, so a
handler can see which way the family went.
A sentence the reader announces after the name.

The popover itself; the trigger and the surface go inside it. It holds whether
the surface is showing and which side it is placed on, and it is the anchor
end of the CSS anchor placement, which lives in the part's own scoped
stylesheet - your `style` and `class` compose untouched.

props.name: open
props.doc: Whether the surface is showing. Omit it and the popover starts closed.

props.name: side
props.doc:
Where the surface is placed against the trigger. It is also written on
`popover.content` as `ui-side`, so styling can follow the placement.

The placement is a CSS anchor, so it holds while the page scrolls and
reflows without any script. The anchor binding and one default
`position-area` per side ship in the parts' own scoped stylesheets, inside
`@layer markless` - so any unlayered rule of yours keyed off `ui-side`
replaces the default without a specificity fight. `--ui-anchor` on
`popover.content` names the anchor for your own `anchor()` geometry.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when the popover opens or closes - including when
Escape or a press outside closes it. Omit it and the popover still opens and
closes; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: The surface's name. Mounting it is what names the surface.
A consumer's `onClick` runs after the popover has opened or closed.

The filled part of the track. The family owns its `style` attribute - the fill
is a `translateX` written from the value - so style this part from a
stylesheet rather than a `style` prop.

The bar's name. Mounting it is what names the `role="progressbar"` element,
and like every other part it carries `ui-progress`, `ui-value`, `ui-min` and
`ui-max` for styling.

The progress bar itself; the label, track and indicator go inside it. It
renders the `role="progressbar"` element and holds the value and range every
other part reads. It sets no `aria-label` of its own - name it with a
`progress.label`, or spread your own label in.

props.name: value
props.doc: How far along the task is. Omit it, or pass `null`, for an unknown amount.

props.name: min
props.doc: The bottom of the range. Omit it and the range starts at 0.

props.name: max
props.doc: The top of the range. Omit it and the range ends at 100.

parts.doc: The full length of the range; the indicator sits inside it.

The current value as text. Left empty it renders the percentage of the range
the bar has covered - the same number the bar reports as `aria-valuetext` -
and nothing at all while the amount is unknown. Pass children to write the
text yourself. Plain text you pass becomes what the bar reports as
`aria-valuetext`, so a reader speaks your wording rather than the percentage.

The box around the code. Give it light-coloured padding of roughly four
modules: the encoded symbol carries no margin of its own, and readers need
that quiet zone to find the code.

A box centred on the code, for a logo. Anything in here is decorative:
the root is `role="img"`, which makes everything inside it presentational,
so put nothing a reader needs to hear in an overlay.
One `<path>` covering every dark module.
The `<svg>` the pattern is drawn in. Its rendered size is CSS.

The code itself; the frame, pattern and any overlay go inside it. It encodes
the value and renders `role="img"`, which makes everything inside it
presentational - give it your own `aria-label` saying what the code is for.

props.name: value
props.doc: The text the code carries - usually a URL.

props.name: recovery
props.doc:
How much of the code can be damaged or covered and still be read:
"low" 7%, "medium" 15%, "quartile" 25%, "high" 30%. Omit it for "medium".
A logo sitting on top of the code needs "quartile" or "high".

parts.doc: Supporting text for the group. It renders its children and changes nothing else.

The group's validation message. Mounting it is what marks the group invalid
for as long as it is in the page, so render it only when there is an error to
show.

One option: its trigger, indicator, label and hidden radio go inside. It
carries the option's `value` and reports `ui-selected` and `ui-disabled`, but
holds no radio semantics itself - those live on the native input inside it.

props.name: value
props.doc: Submitted when this option is the chosen one. Required: no index stands in for it.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can choose this option, and the arrow keys walk past it.

parts.doc:
The visually hidden native radio that carries the option into a form and is
the element a person actually focuses. It takes no configuration of its own:
`name` and `required` come from `radiogroup.root` and `value` from
`radiogroup.item`, so one place decides what a form receives.

One option's chosen mark. Its children render only while that option is the
chosen one, and the element is `aria-hidden`, so the state it draws is never
announced twice.

One option's label. Its `for` points at that option's hidden radio, so
clicking the text chooses the option and focus lands where the arrow keys
expect it.
A consumer's `onClick` runs after the option has been chosen.
The group's name: the element `role="radiogroup"` points its `aria-labelledby` at.

The group: a `role="radiogroup"` element named by `radiogroup.label` through
`aria-labelledby`.

props.name: value
props.doc: The value of the chosen option. Omit it and nothing is chosen.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: Which axis the arrow keys walk. Omit it and the options stack top to bottom.

props.name: loop
props.doc: Arrow past the last option and land on the first. Omit it and the ends still wrap.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can change any option.

props.name: name
props.doc:
The name every option in this group submits under, declared once here rather
than repeated on every option. Omit it and the group submits nothing.

props.name: required
props.doc: A choice is needed before the form submits.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Intended to be called with the new value when a person picks a different
option. Omit it and picking still works; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc:
The popup the options go in. Closed hides it, never detaches it - the
trigger's `aria-controls` points at this element. It owns the arrow, Home,
End, Enter, Space, Escape and typeahead keys while it is showing.

The visually hidden native `<select>` that carries the choice into a form. It
takes no configuration of its own: `name`, `required` and `disabled` come
from `select.root` and the value from whichever option was chosen, so one
place decides what a form receives.

One option. Clicking it, or activating it from the keyboard, chooses it
and closes the popup. It takes focus as the list is walked, but it is never a
tab stop - only `select.trigger` is.

props.name: value
props.doc: Submitted when this option is the chosen one. Required: no index stands in for it.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can choose this option, and the arrow keys walk past it.

parts.doc:
One option's chosen mark. It stays in the page and carries `ui-hidden` while
its option is not the chosen one, and it is `aria-hidden`, so the state it
draws is never announced twice.
The words shown for one option. Plain markup: it decides nothing on its own.
The select's name. Named by `aria-labelledby` from the trigger and the listbox.

The root carries the whole family's configuration and renders no role of its
own, exactly as QDS's `SelectRoot` does. `multiple` is deliberately absent:
it is the one prop that turns `value` into a union and doubles the keyboard
table, and the research note files it as a scope decision for a later tranche.

props.name: value
props.doc: The value of the chosen option. Omit it and nothing is chosen.

props.name: open
props.doc: The popup is showing. Omit it and it starts closed.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can change the choice.

props.name: required
props.doc: A choice is needed before the form submits.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `select.field`.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Intended to be called with the new value when a person chooses a different
option. Omit it and choosing still works; the call site simply does nothing.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.doc: Called when the popup opens or closes.

parts.doc:
The control a person opens the list from, and the family's only tab stop. It
shows the current choice and declares `aria-haspopup="listbox"`; a consumer's
`onClick` and `onKeydown` run after the family's.
Names the slider for a reader: every thumb points its `aria-labelledby` here.

The slider itself; the label, track and thumbs go inside it. It holds the
range and the current value, and the shape of `value` is what decides the
slider: one number for one thumb, a pair for two. The family owns this
element's `style` attribute to carry the filled portion, so style the root
from a stylesheet rather than a `style` prop.

props.name: value
props.doc: Where the slider sits now. A pair means two values. Omit it and it starts at `min`.

props.name: min
props.doc: The bottom of the range. Omit it and the range starts at 0.

props.name: max
props.doc: The top of the range. Omit it and the range ends at 100.

props.name: step
props.doc: The smallest change a person can make. Omit it and it is 1.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: Which axis the slider runs along. Omit it and it runs left to right.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can change the value.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the new value every time it changes, including during a drag.

props.name: onChangeEnd
props.doc: Called once the change settles: the pointer released, or the key that moved it.

parts.doc:
The handle a person drags or arrows, and the `role="slider"` element a reader
announces - a two-value slider has two of them, one per side. The family owns
its `style` attribute to carry the position along the track, so style it from
a stylesheet rather than a `style` prop.

props.name: side
props.doc: Which of the two values this thumb holds. Omit it on a one-value slider.

parts.doc:
The rail, and the hit area a pointer gesture runs on. The family ships no CSS,
so the consumer owes it `position: relative` and `touch-action: none` —
without the second one a touch scrolls the page instead of moving a thumb.

The current value as text: one number, or both separated by an en dash. It
takes no children — a consumer who wants their own wording writes their own
element and reads `ui-value` off it.

One panel. It stays in the page when its tab is not the showing one — `hidden`
decides whether it shows, never an arm — so focus, scroll position and form
state inside a panel all survive a tab change.

props.name: value
props.doc: Names the panel. The trigger part with the same value shows it. Required.

parts.doc: The row of tabs. `role="tablist"`, and the element the arrow keys walk inside.

The tabs themselves; the list, triggers and panels go inside it. It holds
which tab is showing and how the arrow keys walk; a trigger and the panel it
shows find each other by matching `value`, never by position.

props.name: value
props.doc:
The value of the tab that is showing. Omit it and no tab shows: a tab is
named by its `value`, and nothing counts positions for you.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: Which axis the arrow keys walk. Omit it and the tabs run left to right.

props.name: loop
props.doc: Arrow past the last tab and land on the first. Omit it and the ends stop.

props.name: selectOnFocus
props.doc: Arrowing to a tab shows it. Turn it off and arrowing only moves focus; Enter or Space shows it.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when a person changes tab. Omit it and the tabs
still change; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc:
One tab. `role="tab"` makes every child of this element presentational, so it
takes label content only — a close button or a link inside a tab is stripped
of its own semantics, and has to be a sibling of the tab instead.

A consumer's `onClick`, `onFocus` and `onKeydown` all run after the family's.

props.name: value
props.doc: Names the tab. The content part with the same value is the panel it shows. Required.

parts.doc:
Supporting text for the box, named by the control's `aria-describedby`. Mount
it alongside `textbox.error` and the control names both, the error first.

The validation message, named by the control's `aria-describedby` ahead of
`textbox.description`. Mounting it is what marks the control invalid - it
reports `aria-invalid` for as long as this part is in the page - so render it
only when there is an error to show.

The control a person types into. `disabled`, `required` and `readonly` may be
set here as well as on the root, and a restriction set in either place stands:
a part can add a restriction, never remove one.
The box's name. Its `for` points at the control, so clicking the text focuses it.

The text box itself; the label, the control, and any description or error go
inside it. It holds the text and the restrictions, and reports `ui-disabled`,
`ui-required`, `ui-readonly` and `ui-empty` for styling. Put either a
`textbox.input` or a `textbox.textarea` inside - the root renders no control
of its own.

props.name: value
props.doc: The text the box shows. Omit it and the box starts empty.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can type in the control, and it drops out of the tab order.

props.name: required
props.doc: The control must hold text before a form submits.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: The text can be read and selected but not changed.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by whichever control the family renders.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new text as a person types. Omit it and the box still works;
the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: The same control over more than one line.

One message's row. Everything it shows comes from the `toast` record it is
given. It reports `ui-tone` and `ui-front`, and the family owns its `style`
attribute to carry the stacking, so style it from a stylesheet rather than a
`style` prop.

props.name: toast
props.doc: The message this row shows.

props.name: index
props.doc: Where it stands in the stack: 0 is the front one.

parts.doc:
The button that dismisses the message it sits in. It takes no id: the item
around it holds one, the same way `select.itemindicator` reads its option.

The line under the headline. Leave it empty and it renders the description the
record carries; give it children and they are shown instead.

The tone's mark. Leave it empty and it renders the character minted for the
tone. It is `aria-hidden`, because the words carry the meaning, not the symbol.

The message's headline. Leave it empty and it renders the title the record
carries; give it children and they are shown instead.

The region every message appears in. It is on the page before the first
message, because a live region added at the same moment as its text is not
announced.

There is no `visible` prop: the root renders no rows of its own, so how many
messages show is decided by the consumer's own repeat. `toaster.shown(queue, n)`
is the cap they write against.

Supporting text for the switch, named by the trigger's `aria-describedby`.
Mount it alongside `toggle.error` and the trigger names both, the error first.

The validation message, named by the trigger's `aria-describedby` ahead of
`toggle.description`. Mounting it is what marks the switch invalid - the
trigger reports `aria-invalid` for as long as this part is in the page - so
render it only when there is an error to show.

The visually hidden native input that carries the switch into a form. It takes
no configuration of its own: `name`, `value` and `required` come from
`toggle.root`, so one place decides what a form receives.
The switch's label. Its `for` points at `toggle.trigger`, so clicking the text flips it.

The switch itself; the trigger, thumb, label, messages and field go inside it.
It holds whether the switch is on and the form details `toggle.field`
submits, so one place decides what a form receives.

props.name: checked
props.doc: Whether the switch reads as on. Omit it and the switch starts off.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can flip the switch, and `toggle.trigger` is disabled outright.

props.name: required
props.doc: Marks the hidden `toggle.field` input required, so a form refuses to submit with the switch off.

props.name: name
props.doc: Submitted under this name by `toggle.field`.

props.name: value
props.doc: Submitted instead of the browser default `"on"`.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when a person flips the switch. Omit it and the
switch still works; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc: The moving piece inside the trigger. It renders an element and nothing else.
A consumer's `onClick` runs after the switch has flipped.

One toggle button. A real `<button aria-pressed>`, not a switch: a switch is a
setting that takes effect at once, which is what `toggle` is for, while this
is a control a person presses on and off inside a set.

The button's own content is its accessible name, so it takes label content and
needs no label part. A consumer's `onClick`, `onFocus` and `onKeydown` all run
after the family's.

props.name: value
props.doc: What this item contributes to the group's value. Required: position is never identity.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can press this item, and the arrow keys walk past it.

parts.doc:
The hidden input that carries one pressed item into a form. Written inside the
item whose value it submits, it takes no configuration of its own: `name`
comes from `togglegroup.root` and `value` from `togglegroup.item`, so one
place decides what a form receives. It is in the page only while its item is
pressed, which is what makes a `multiple` group submit its name once per
pressed value with no special handling.
The group's name: the element `role="group"` points its `aria-labelledby` at.

A set of toggle buttons - text alignment, or bold/italic/underline. The group
is a `role="group"` element named by `togglegroup.label`, and every item
inside it is a real button reporting `aria-pressed`.

Arrows move focus and never press: that is the whole difference from
`radiogroup`, where an arrow also chooses. Enter and Space press the focused
item, because the item is a button and the browser activates it.

props.name: value
props.doc:
The pressed value, or the pressed values when the group is `multiple`.
Omit it and nothing is pressed.

props.name: multiple
props.doc: Any number of items may be pressed at once. Omit it and pressing one unpresses the rest.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: Which axis the arrow keys walk. Omit it and the items run left to right.

props.name: loop
props.doc: Arrow past the last item and land on the first. Omit it and the ends stop.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can press any item.

props.name: required
props.doc:
The group keeps at least one pressed item: pressing the last pressed one
does nothing. Omit it and a person can leave the group with nothing pressed.

props.name: name
props.doc:
The name every `togglegroup.itemfield` submits under, declared once here
rather than repeated per item. Omit it and the group submits nothing.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Intended to be called with what is pressed now - one value, or the whole
list when the group is `multiple`, and `''` or `[]` once nothing is left
pressed. The shape mirrors the shape `value` was written in. Omit it and
pressing still works; the call site simply does nothing.

parts.doc:
The tip. It is text, not a surface a person can work in: no links, no buttons,
nothing to focus.

**Write it after `tooltip.trigger`.** A CSS anchor has to be laid out strictly
before the element that points at it. An ordinary in-flow trigger satisfies
that from anywhere in the markup, so the order is only advice - until you
absolutely position the trigger yourself, at which point a tip written first
silently lands at its containing block instead of beside it. CSS has no way to
report that, so put the tip last and the question never comes up.

It stays in the page when the tooltip is hidden - `hidden` decides whether it
shows, never an arm - because the trigger points at its minted id and because
an elevated element removed from the document while showing leaves the overlay
stack's marks behind.

Its `position: absolute` and anchor binding live in the part's own scoped
stylesheet - your `style` and `class` compose untouched. Everything about
where the tip lands - `position-area`, `@position-try`, `position-visibility`,
offsets - is your CSS, keyed off `ui-side`.

The tooltip itself; the trigger and the tip go inside it, in that order. It
holds whether the tip is showing, how long the pointer has to rest before it
shows, and which side it sits on.

The pointer handlers live here rather than on the trigger, so moving the
pointer from the trigger onto the tip never counts as leaving.

props.name: open
props.doc: Whether the tooltip is showing. Omit it and it starts hidden.

props.name: delay
props.doc:
How long the pointer must rest on the trigger before the tooltip shows, in
milliseconds. Omit it and it is 600. Focus shows it at once, with no wait.

props.name: side
props.doc:
Where the tooltip sits against the trigger. It is written on
`tooltip.content` as `ui-side`; the placement itself is your CSS.

props.name: onChange
props.doc:
Called with the new value when the tooltip shows or hides, including when
Escape or a press elsewhere hides it.

parts.doc:
The control the tooltip describes. It carries the CSS anchor the tip is
placed against, declared in the part's own scoped stylesheet - your `style`
and `class` compose untouched.

It points at the tip with `aria-describedby` at all times, showing or not: a
directly referenced hidden element still contributes its text to the
description, so tabbing to the trigger conveys the tip without it ever being
shown.

An icon-only trigger needs its own accessible name - write `aria-label` on it.
The tooltip describes the control; it never names it.

One node. A node that holds children renders a `tree.itemcontent` with more
`tree.item`s inside it, and each of those roots its own instance.

props.name: open
props.doc: This node's children are showing. Omit it and the node starts closed.

props.name: leaf
props.doc:
This node has no children. A leaf reports no open state at all, which is
the WAI-ARIA rule a reader needs to tell "nothing to open" from "closed".

props.name: level
props.doc:
How deep this node sits, counting from 1. It is written rather than read
off the enclosing node, because a component that roots an instance of a
family cannot also read the enclosing instance of that same family.

props.name: onChange
props.doc: Called with the new state when a person opens or closes this node.

parts.doc:
The container of one node's children, `role="group"`. It stays in the page
when the node is closed - `hidden` decides whether it shows, never an arm -
so the ids inside it, the focus in it, and the widget instances under it all
survive a close.
A decorative open/closed marker. It is hidden from the accessibility tree.
The node's name. The trigger points at it, and typeahead matches on it.
The control that opens and closes one node. A consumer's `onClick` runs after.
The tree's own heading. It does not name the tree; see `TreeRootProps`.

The tree container. It carries `role="tree"` and owns the one tab stop the
whole tree has, plus the typeahead buffer every row types into.

The tree's accessible name comes through `{...rest}` as a plain `aria-label`:
naming it from `tree.label` would need an IDREF handle read on a widget root,
which is `MARKLESS_ELEMENT_HANDLE_IDREF_WIDGET_ROOT` today..

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Nobody can open or close anything while this is set.
